zupix

zupix reads and writes PNG, JPEG, WebP and QOI images. Each of those formats is already readable from R, but through a system library (libpng, libjpeg, libwebp) or ImageMagick, which has to be installed before the package can be built from source. And images arrive from the network, from PDFs and from users, so decoding one is parsing input nobody has checked.

zupix compiles every codec into the package and treats every file as hostile:

  • No system library. Installing zupix needs a C compiler and the zlib R is built with, nothing else. PNG, JPEG and WebP decode through Wuffs and QOI through qoi.h; encoding goes through zupix’s own PNG writer, libjpeg-turbo, libwebp and qoi.h.
  • Built for hostile input. Wuffs’s decoders are memory-safe by construction, QOI streams are checked complete before qoi.h decodes them, and every size an image declares is checked against pix_limits() before anything is allocated. zupix’s own metadata scanners are fuzzed.
  • The pixels the file holds. No colour management, gamma or orientation is applied unless you ask. ICC profiles and EXIF blocks come out as raw bytes, and the EXIF orientation is applied only with orient = TRUE.
  • Familiar shapes. Images decode to a nativeRaster or an array, as the png package returns them, at 8 or 16 bits, and the writers take the same shapes back.
  • A C interface for other packages. The same codecs are available to C code through a registered function table.

Installation

zupix is not on CRAN yet. Install the development version from GitHub:

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("pedrobtz/zupix")

Usage 

library(zupix)

pix_info() reads what an image is from its header, without decoding a pixel. It takes any number of files.

f <- system.file("extdata", "gradient.png", package = "zupix")
pix_info(f)[c("format", "width", "height", "bits", "colour_type", "alpha")]
#>   format width height bits colour_type alpha
#> 1    png    48     32    8         rgb FALSE

pix_read() decodes to a nativeRaster by default, ready for grid::grid.raster(). Ask for "integer" or "double" to work with the values; the shape is height x width x channels.

img <- pix_read(f, as = "integer")
dim(img)
#> [1] 32 48  3
img[1:2, 1:3, 1]
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3]
#> [1,]    0    5   11
#> [2,]    0    5   11

The writers take the same shapes. Here the image goes out as a JPEG that carries an EXIF orientation of 6, “rotate 90 degrees clockwise to display”. Reading it back returns the pixels as stored unless orient = TRUE says to apply that.

exif <- as.raw(c(0x49, 0x49, 0x2a, 0, 8, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0x12, 1, 3, 0, 1, 0,
                 0, 0, 6, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0))
jpg <- pix_write_jpeg(img, quality = 90L, exif = exif)
pix_info(jpg)$orientation
#> [1] 6
dim(pix_read(jpg, as = "integer"))
#> [1] 32 48  3
dim(pix_read(jpg, as = "integer", orient = TRUE))
#> [1] 48 32  3

Every size an image declares is checked before memory is allocated. A breach is a zupix_limit_error that names the limit, raised before any pixel memory exists.

pix_read(f, limits = pix_limits(max_pixels = 1000))
#> Error in `pix_read()`:
#> ! PNG has 1,536 pixels, more than `max_pixels` (1,000).

Every function starts with pix_, and every writer is pix_write_ and a format; pix_write() picks one from the file’s extension.

Acknowledgements

zupix is built on Wuffs (The Wuffs Authors), libjpeg-turbo, libwebp (Google) and qoi.h (Dominic Szablewski), bundled under their own licences (see inst/COPYRIGHTS). This software is based in part on the work of the Independent JPEG Group.

It is tested against PngSuite (Willem van Schaik), libjpeg-turbo’s and libwebp’s test images and the QOI test images, with the png, jpeg, webp and qoi packages and libjpeg-turbo’s djpeg as reference decoders.
